# Regulatory Institutions in the Domestic Environment {#chap-domestic}  
  
## Objectives of Regulating Financial Institutions  
  
A close study of banking regulation in Nigeria indicates the intended  
objectives include:  
  
- Promotion of monetary and economic stability  
- Protection of depositors and investors  
- Prevention or minimisation of systemic failure  
- Promotion of market integrity and discipline  
- Maintenance of uniformity and standardisation of practice  
- Maintenance of responsible corporate governance  
- Maintenance and restoration of public confidence in the system  
- Encouragement of banking habit and culture  
- Instilling competitive equity (a level playing field)  
- Restraint on certain activities  
- General consumer protection  
- Efficiency in the system and development of the economy  
- Better service delivery  
  
## The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) {#sec-cbn}  
  
The CBN is the apex regulatory authority in the Nigerian banking  
sector. Its functions are:  
  
**(a) Issuance of legal tender currency.** The Bank assumed currency  
issue and distribution in 1959, replacing the West African Currency  
Board pound with the Nigerian pound. The decimal denominations (naira  
and kobo) were introduced in 1973; the ₦20 note in 1976; a colour  
swap in 1984 to discourage hoarding and counterfeiting; a 1991 reform  
phasing out 2k and 5k coins, redesigning 1k, 10k and 25k coins, coining  
50k and ₦1, and issuing the ₦50 note; then ₦100 and ₦200 notes in  
December 1999 and November 2000, and the ₦500 note in 2001.  
  
**(b) Maintenance of external reserves.** To safeguard the  
international value of the currency, the CBN manages the country's  
foreign exchange and is involved in debt management.  
  
**(c) Debt management.** The CBN historically managed domestic debt  
and serviced external debt on the advice of the Federal Ministry of  
Finance — advising on timing and size of new instruments, advertising  
public subscriptions, redeeming matured stock, paying interest and  
principal, and sensitising government on debt and deficit  
implications. In 2001 this responsibility transferred to the Debt  
Management Office (DMO).  
  
**(d) Foreign exchange management.** Acquisition and deployment of  
foreign exchange resources to reduce the destabilising effects of  
short-term capital flows, ensuring disbursement aligns with economic  
priorities and the annual foreign exchange budget to maintain the  
balance-of-payments position and naira stability.  
  
**(e) Promotion of monetary stability and a sound financial system.**  
Price stability is indispensable for money to perform as medium of  
exchange, store of value, standard of deferred payments and unit of  
account. Since 30 June 1993 the CBN has used market-based monetary  
policy, with Open Market Operations (OMO) as the principal instrument.  
  
**(f) Banker and financial adviser to the Federal Government.** The  
CBN undertakes most Federal Government banking business, provides  
services to State and Local Governments, finances temporary budget  
shortfalls through Ways and Means Advances (within legal limits), and  
acts as issuing house for government debt instruments.  
  
**(g) Banker and lender of last resort to banks.** The CBN maintains  
current accounts for deposit money banks, provides clearing-house  
facilities, undertakes trade finance on behalf of banks' customers,  
and provides temporary accommodation as lender of last resort.  
  
## Nigerian Deposit Insurance Corporation (NDIC) {#sec-ndic}  
  
The NDIC is an autonomous body acting as a supervisory authority over  
licensed banks. It provides a financial guarantee to depositors and  
ensures banks comply with regulations fostering safety and soundness.  
  
### Rationale for the deposit insurance scheme  
  
The scheme was established in 1989 under Decree No. 22 of 1988, for  
four reasons:  
  
1. **Lessons of history** — in the 1950s, 21 of 25 indigenous banks  
   failed and small depositors suffered untold hardship.  
2. **International precedent** — Czechoslovakia established the first  
   nationwide scheme in 1924 to revitalise banking after World War I;  
   the US established the FDIC in 1933 in response to banking collapse  
   and panic.  
3. **Structural Adjustment Programme (1986)** — deregulation and  
   liberalised licensing implied more banks to supervise; an explicit  
   deposit insurance scheme with supervisory powers was expected to  
   complement the CBN, enabling more frequent routine and special  
   examinations.  
4. **Failure resolution** — government had previously been unwilling  
   to let any bank fail, propping up inefficient (often state-owned)  
   banks. The Corporation administers deposit protection and provides  
   a vehicle for resolving badly managed insolvent banks.  
  
### Mandates of the NDIC  
  
- **Deposit guarantee**: depositors are protected against loss of  
  insured deposits when a bank cannot meet its obligations.  
- **Bank supervision**: protects depositors, ensures safety and  
  soundness, reduces the risk of failure, and checks unsafe practices.  
- **Failure resolution**: ensures failing institutions are resolved  
  in a timely, efficient manner.  
- **Bank liquidation**: orderly closure of failed institutions with  
  minimum disruption, cost-effective realisation of assets, and  
  settlement of claims to depositors, creditors and shareholders.  
  
### Functions of the NDIC (Section 2, NDIC Act 2006)  
  
- Insuring all deposit liabilities of licensed banks and other covered  
  financial institutions to engender confidence  
- Giving financial and technical assistance to eligible insured  
  institutions in the interest of depositors  
- Guaranteeing payment to depositors up to the statutory maximum where  
  an insured institution suspends payments  
- Assisting monetary authorities in formulating and implementing  
  policies for sound banking and fair competition  
- Pursuing any other measures necessary to achieve its functions  
  
## Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) {#sec-sec}  
  
The SEC is the apex regulatory institution of the Nigerian capital  
market, playing a role parallel to the CBN's in the money market.  
  
### Objectives  
  
1. **Investor protection** — financial assets cannot have their worth  
   determined by physical examination, and financial services are  
   complex, so issuers must provide relevant, timely, adequate  
   information; protection also targets fraud, false claims, price  
   manipulation and misuse of undisclosed price-sensitive information.  
2. **Capital market development** — creating awareness of the market  
   as a source of investment finance, researching market efficiency,  
   introducing new instruments, and advising government on capital  
   market issues.  
  
### Functions of the SEC  
  
- Determining the price, amount and timing of securities offered by  
  sale or subscription  
- Registering securities proposed for public offer  
- Maintaining surveillance to ensure orderly, fair and equitable  
  dealings  
- Registering stock exchanges, registrars, securities dealers and  
  other market operators to maintain standards and professionalism  
- Protecting market integrity against insider trading abuses  
- Acting as apex regulator over the Nigerian Stock Exchange and its  
  branches  
- Reviewing, approving and regulating business combinations  
- Creating the atmosphere for orderly growth and development of the  
  capital market  
  
### How SEC protects the investing public  
  
- Full disclosure in prospectuses  
- Adequate and timely financial reporting  
- Fair and equitable issuance of securities  
- Fair trading practices  
  
## National Insurance Commission (NAICOM) {#sec-naicom}  
  
NAICOM was established in 1997 by the NAICOM Act No. 1 of 1997 to  
enhance the effective administration, supervision, regulation and  
control of insurance business in Nigeria.  
  
### Services rendered by NAICOM  
  
- Establishing standards for the conduct of insurance business  
- Approving insurance premium rates and commission rates for all  
  classes of business  
- Ensuring adequate protection of strategic government assets  
- Regulating transactions between Nigerian insurers/reinsurers and  
  those outside Nigeria  
- Advising the Federal Government on insurance matters  
- Approving standards, conditions and warranties for all classes of  
  insurance  
- Protecting policyholders, beneficiaries and third parties  
- Publishing annual reports and statistics on the insurance industry  
- Liaising with government bodies on insurance matters in technical  
  agreements to which Nigeria is a signatory  
- Contributing to the educational programmes of the Chartered  
  Insurance Institute of Nigeria and the West African Insurance  
  Institute  
  
### Customers and performance targets  
  
NAICOM serves insurance and reinsurance companies, brokers, loss  
adjusters and agents, the insuring public, and all tiers of  
government. Targets include:  
  
1. A peaceful, orderly, well-regulated insurance industry, with claims  
   paid within 3 months (90 days)  
2. Registration of companies within 2 months (60 days)
